title: Mansa Musa's Gold in Cairo
text:
In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the empire of Mali in West Africa, set out on the pilgrimage to Mecca. His caravan crossed the Sahara with a huge following and a great quantity of gold, which came from the mines of the West African interior. When he reached Cairo, then the largest city of the Islamic world, his visit became legendary.

The Egyptian official and scholar al-Umari, who wrote some years later and interviewed people who had met the king, reports what happened. Mansa Musa and his entourage spent and gave away gold lavishly, to officials, to the sultan's court and in the markets. So much gold entered the city that its value fell. Al-Umari says that the price of gold in Egypt had been high before, but it dropped after the visit and had still not recovered twelve years later.

The chroniclers also record a sequel. On his way home, Mansa Musa's party had spent so much that he had to borrow money from Cairo merchants at high rates. The visit made Mali famous across the Mediterranean, and a few decades later European mapmakers drew Mansa Musa enthroned in the middle of Africa, holding a nugget of gold.
lesson: What is scarce is valuable; flood a market with it and its worth drops. Abundance spent without thought can undermine the very wealth it displays.
source: Ibn Fadl Allah al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar fi Mamalik al-Amsar; translated in N. Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
caveat: The size of Mansa Musa's caravan and the amounts of gold are uncertain and often exaggerated in modern retellings.
